learning_paths.title: Start Here
learning_paths.plain_language_goal: Understand the problem OIEC solves and complete one safe read-only task.
learning_paths.completion_evidence: The reader can explain the governed loop and run a read-only inspection command.

learning_paths.title: Understand
learning_paths.plain_language_goal: Turn a broad request into an inspectable problem model.
learning_paths.completion_evidence: The reader can distinguish evidence from a proposal and draw an OURD map.

learning_paths.title: Experiment
learning_paths.plain_language_goal: Vary one useful dimension while preserving declared invariants.
learning_paths.completion_evidence: The reader can define a baseline, one variation, and a comparison result.

learning_paths.title: Act Safely
learning_paths.plain_language_goal: Compile an exact bounded proposal and inspect its authority and evidence gates.
learning_paths.completion_evidence: The reader can explain scope, risk, approval, evidence, and rollback.

learning_paths.title: Learn and Improve
learning_paths.plain_language_goal: Record failures, retrieve known work, adapt one dimension, and close the loop.
learning_paths.completion_evidence: The reader can assemble and explain the complete governed improvement loop.

tutorials.title: Welcome
tutorials.reader_outcome: Explain what OIEC is for without relying on acronyms.

tutorials.title: Install
tutorials.reader_outcome: Install the package and identify the five command names.

tutorials.title: First Read-Only Task
tutorials.reader_outcome: Inspect a repository without granting write authority.

tutorials.title: Evidence
tutorials.reader_outcome: Separate source facts, model proposals, and verified observations.

tutorials.title: OURD
tutorials.reader_outcome: Map objects, boundaries, relations, and unresolved questions.

tutorials.title: IURM
tutorials.reader_outcome: Design a one-variable experiment with a stable baseline.

tutorials.title: EGCF
tutorials.reader_outcome: Read and assemble an inspectable semantic command.

tutorials.title: EON
tutorials.reader_outcome: Inspect an exact proposed mutation before it can execute.

tutorials.title: CFEL
tutorials.reader_outcome: Record a failed expectation so blind retries stop.

tutorials.title: SAA
tutorials.reader_outcome: Search qualified knowledge before inventing a replacement.

tutorials.title: Adaptation
tutorials.reader_outcome: Adapt one declared dimension without hiding structural changes.

tutorials.title: A/B Evidence
tutorials.reader_outcome: Compare a candidate with a frozen baseline using named evidence.

tutorials.title: Closed Loop
tutorials.reader_outcome: Promote and re-retrieve only evidence-qualified knowledge.

tutorials.title: Build a Workflow
tutorials.reader_outcome: Combine understanding, experimentation, action, verification, and learning.

task_routes.plain_language_goal: Inspect structure, owners, and evidence without changing files.

task_routes.title: Debug a bug
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Turn a symptom into competing hypotheses and discriminating tests.

task_routes.title: Safely modify files
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Grant a narrow write boundary and verify an exact candidate.

task_routes.title: Write a report
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Separate supported claims from proposals and limitations.

task_routes.title: Run an experiment
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Hold a baseline, vary one dimension, and record observations.

task_routes.title: Compare algorithms
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Compare qualified candidates under the same evidence contract.

task_routes.title: Use OIEC with Ollama
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Connect a local OpenAI-compatible provider without changing governance.

task_routes.title: Understand a failure
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Decode a refusal or failed expectation and identify the next safe step.

task_routes.title: Build my own command
task_routes.plain_language_goal: Assemble an EGCF command from semantic parts rather than memorizing flags.

case_studies.title: Why will the lamp not turn on?
case_studies.problem: A lamp remains dark after a bulb replacement.

case_studies.title: Why did the bread fail?
case_studies.problem: A loaf is dense despite following the recipe.

case_studies.title: Controller oscillation
case_studies.problem: A temperature controller oscillates around its setpoint.

case_studies.title: Unexpected brake vibration
case_studies.problem: A vehicle vibrates during braking under limited conditions.

case_studies.title: Competing scientific hypotheses
case_studies.problem: Several explanations fit the first observation.

case_studies.title: Parser regression
case_studies.problem: A parser changes precedence after a recent edit.

case_studies.title: Unsupported report claim
case_studies.problem: A report contains a confident claim without adequate evidence.

case_studies.title: Choosing between two processes
case_studies.problem: Two workflows promise improvement but use different measures.

invention_timeline.title: Make intent inspectable
invention_timeline.problem: Broad human requests hide assumptions, scope, and ambiguity.
invention_timeline.response: HRT records a reviewable interpretation before deeper modeling.

invention_timeline.title: Model the territory
invention_timeline.problem: A plausible first solution can hide missing objects and dependencies.
invention_timeline.response: OURD decomposes the problem into orthogonal, uniquely identified components while preserving their relations, dependencies, boundaries, exclusions, and unknowns.

invention_timeline.title: Learn through controlled variation
invention_timeline.problem: Changing several dimensions at once produces weak causal evidence.
invention_timeline.response: IURM selects baselines, invariants, dimensions, and responses.

invention_timeline.title: Separate reasoning from mutation
invention_timeline.problem: A good idea is not yet an authorized, source-bound action.
invention_timeline.response: EON binds exact targets, state, authority, evidence, tests, and rollback.

invention_timeline.title: Stop blind retries
invention_timeline.problem: A failed approach can recur with different wording but no new evidence.
invention_timeline.response: CFEL records expectation, observation, collision, and next learning constraints.

invention_timeline.title: Retrieve before reinventing
invention_timeline.problem: Qualified solutions and known failures are wasted when every task starts from generation.
invention_timeline.response: SAA represents, qualifies, searches, adapts, and re-retrieves reusable structures.

acronyms.expansion: OIEC (canonical project name; no expanded form is declared in current source)
acronyms.short_meaning: The governed architecture that separates understanding, evidence, authority, action, and learning.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A careful workshop process with separate planning, inspection, permission, and quality-control stations.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The repository-wide architecture name. Documentation must not invent an expansion that the source does not declare.

acronyms.short_meaning: The bounded state-transition part of OIEC-STM-Agent.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A turnstile that admits only a checked transition rather than any movement.
acronyms.formal_meaning: STM is the State Transition Machine: the bounded-transition layer that governs admissible state changes; it is not ordinary conversational short-term memory.

acronyms.short_meaning: A bounded additive layer for generating and comparing reasoning candidates.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Several engineers propose explanations while a separate process checks evidence and authority.
acronyms.formal_meaning: OIEC-SR proposes hypotheses and evidence requests but cannot enlarge external authority.

acronyms.short_meaning: Decomposes a problem into orthogonal, uniquely identified relational components and the relations between them.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: List every part of a lamp circuit before blaming the bulb.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A canonical decomposition into orthogonal, uniquely identified relational components, together with their relations, dependencies, boundaries, exclusions, and unresolved relations.

acronyms.short_meaning: Chooses useful controlled variations that reduce uncertainty.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Change one recipe variable while keeping the rest stable.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A bounded experiment model containing dimensions, invariants, baselines, variations, and responses.

acronyms.short_meaning: Turns a proposal into an exact action identity with authority and evidence requirements.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A repair order naming the exact machine, part, permission, checks, and rollback.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A content-addressed action boundary bound to source state, targets, authority, risk, evidence, and rollback.

acronyms.expansion: Collision, Failure, Evidence, and Learning Feedback
acronyms.short_meaning: Records what failed or contradicted expectations so the system does not retry blindly.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A mechanic writes down that replacing the bulb did not solve the fault.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A source-bound feedback record connecting expectations, observations, collisions, failures, and reusable learning.

acronyms.short_meaning: Compiles semantic commands into inspectable governed plans.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A work order that states the job, location, risk, proof, approval, and rollback.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The typed command fabric that compiles namespace and verb intent into governed plan nodes and evidence requirements.

acronyms.short_meaning: Makes the request, assumptions, scope, and ambiguity explicit.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Repeat a repair request back to the owner before touching the machine.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The inspectable interpretation record that precedes OURD modeling.

acronyms.short_meaning: Produces tests, counterexamples, coverage, and evidence gates.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A test bench designed to reveal whether a repair actually works.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The evidence-production service for qualification, falsification, and bounded gate decisions.

acronyms.short_meaning: Determines the supported boundary of a claim or model.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Mark the operating range in which a machine was actually tested.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A bounded reasoning stage that derives the domain on which later claims may be evaluated.

acronyms.short_meaning: Restricts active dimensions to a tractable and justified set.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Test temperature before changing temperature, flour, timing, and humidity together.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A bounded reasoning stage that limits dimensions before experimentation or action.

acronyms.short_meaning: Represents, qualifies, searches, and adapts reusable algorithmic structures.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Search a repair manual for a proven procedure before inventing one.
acronyms.formal_meaning: A staged algebra and store for canonical, semantically resolved, evidence-qualified algorithm and reasoning structures.

acronyms.short_meaning: A text interface for running a program with commands and options.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Writing a precise work order instead of using a control panel.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The package exposes agent, EGCF, and GUI launch commands through project scripts.

acronyms.short_meaning: A visual interface using windows, panels, buttons, and diagrams.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A workshop control panel rather than a typed work order.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The Tkinter engineering workbench exposed by the OIEC GUI entry points.

acronyms.short_meaning: A one-way dependency graph with no loops.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A set of recipe steps where no later step can become its own prerequisite.
acronyms.formal_meaning: Used for ordered plans, prerequisites, and workflow dependencies that must remain cycle-free.

acronyms.short_meaning: A design document used to specify Python changes and conventions.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A formally reviewed proposal for changing workshop standards.
acronyms.formal_meaning: Packaging documentation refers to PEP 517 build-system behavior.

acronyms.short_meaning: The Python standard that defines a build-system interface for source trees and frontend tools.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A standard handoff form between a workshop design and any approved builder.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The repository declares a PEP 517-compatible custom build backend in pyproject.toml.

acronyms.short_meaning: A platform interface used to create graphics contexts, including headless contexts.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: The adapter that connects a renderer to a display or headless surface.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The visual workbench may use a ModernGL EGL backend for headless rendering.

acronyms.short_meaning: A defined way for software components to communicate.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: A labeled socket whose allowed shape and signals are documented.
acronyms.formal_meaning: The repository uses local Python APIs and OpenAI-compatible provider APIs behind governed boundaries.

acronyms.short_meaning: A binary-level compatibility contract between compiled components.
acronyms.everyday_analogy: Machine parts that fit because dimensions and connection rules match.
acronyms.formal_meaning: ABI appears in technical compatibility discussions and must not be confused with a source-level API.

references.title: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th Edition
references.authors: Len Bass, Paul Clements, and Rick Kazman
references.summary: The textbook treats architecture as the disciplined management of quality attributes, trade-offs, lifecycle change, and organizational value.

references.title: NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1: Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems
references.authors: Ron Ross, Mark Winstead, and Michael McEvilley
references.summary: NIST frames trustworthiness as a whole-system engineering concern that must be addressed through requirements, architecture, implementation, verification, validation, and lifecycle evidence.

references.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework 1.1
references.authors: Murugiah Souppaya, Karen Scarfone, and Donna Dodson
references.summary: The Secure Software Development Framework recommends integrating secure practices into the development lifecycle and using a shared vocabulary for producers, acquirers, and reviewers.

references.title: RFC 2119 and BCP 14 requirement language
references.summary: The RFC distinguishes absolute requirements, recommendations, and optional behaviour so readers can tell policy force from ordinary emphasis.

references.title: Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety
references.summary: Leveson argues that complex software-intensive systems should be understood through interacting controls, constraints, feedback, and sociotechnical context rather than through isolated component failure alone.

references.title: Design and Analysis of Experiments, 10th Edition
references.summary: Montgomery presents experimental design as a disciplined way to vary factors, measure responses, discover interactions, and draw objective engineering conclusions.

references.title: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems
references.authors: Jerome H. Saltzer and Michael D. Schroeder
references.summary: The classic protection principles include least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, economy of mechanism, and explicit design rather than secrecy.

references.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook
references.summary: NASA explains systems engineering as a lifecycle discipline that connects stakeholder needs, requirements, design, implementation, verification, validation, and technical decision-making.

references.title: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: Developing a Keyboard Interface
references.authors: World Wide Web Consortium Web Accessibility Initiative
references.summary: W3C guidance explains that interactive interfaces need predictable keyboard movement, visible focus, and controls whose behaviour is understandable without relying on a mouse.

references.title: RFC 8785: JSON Canonicalization Scheme
references.authors: Anders Rundgren, Bruce Jordan, and Samuel Erdtman
references.summary: The RFC defines a repeatable JSON representation so hashing and signing use the same bytes even when ordinary serializers could choose different layouts.

references.title: Atomic Commit in SQLite
references.summary: SQLite describes atomic commit as making a transaction appear fully applied or not applied at all, including recovery when interruption happens mid-write.

references.title: Git Internals: Git Objects
references.summary: Git stores content-addressed objects whose identifiers depend on content, allowing snapshots and relationships to be checked rather than trusted by name.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management
references.summary: NIST treats logs as evidence that must be generated, protected, reviewed, and managed across a lifecycle so events can support detection and investigation.

references.title: Python Standard Library: dataclasses
references.summary: Python documents data classes as a way to declare named fields and generate standard methods, making record structure explicit and inspectable.

references.title: RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation Data Interchange Format
references.summary: The RFC defines JSON as a text format for structured values and specifies the grammar needed for different implementations to exchange the same information.

references.title: NIST Technical Note 1297: Measurement Uncertainty Terminology
references.authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
references.summary: NIST explains uncertainty as information about the spread of values that could reasonably describe a measured result, rather than as a vague feeling of doubt.

glossary.ADR: Architecture Decision Record: a short document that records a significant design choice, its context, and its consequences.
glossary.API: A defined way for software components to communicate.
glossary.BCP: Best Current Practice: an Internet standards document that records widely accepted operational guidance.
glossary.C0: Capability class 0: observation only; it may inspect information but cannot create proposals or change the workspace.
glossary.C1: Capability class 1: analysis and internal proposal creation without ordinary workspace mutation.
glossary.C2: Capability class 2: simulation in a disposable, synthetic, or otherwise isolated environment.
glossary.C3: Capability class 3: local workspace mutation through the governed EON execution boundary with exact authority and approval.
glossary.C4: Capability class 4: mutation of an external system; EGCFv1 currently fails closed for this class.
glossary.C5: Capability class 5: critical or destructive mutation; EGCFv1 currently fails closed for this class.
glossary.CERTIFIED: A status label claiming that named certification checks and approvals have been satisfied; the label is trustworthy only when it is tied to current evidence.
glossary.C0-C5: The full capability-class ladder, from observation-only C0 through critical or destructive C5 operations.
glossary.C2-C5: Capability classes 2 through 5: simulation, local mutation, external mutation, and critical or destructive mutation.
glossary.C3-C5: The mutation-capable classes: governed local mutation, external mutation, and critical or destructive mutation.
glossary.CAD: Computer-Aided Design: software and data used to create or analyse engineered geometry.
glossary.CFEL: Records what failed or contradicted expectations so the system does not retry blindly.
glossary.CLI: A text interface for running a program with commands and options.
glossary.DAG: A one-way dependency graph with no loops.
glossary.EGCF: Compiles semantic commands into inspectable governed plans.
glossary.EON: Turns a proposal into an exact action identity with authority and evidence requirements.
glossary.GIF: Graphics Interchange Format: a bitmap image format that can contain simple animation.
glossary.GLB: The binary container form of glTF, used to package 3D scenes and assets into one file.
glossary.GLTF: GL Transmission Format: a standard format for transmitting 3D scenes and models.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: a processor designed for highly parallel work such as graphics and machine-learning calculations.
glossary.GUI: A visual interface using windows, panels, buttons, and diagrams.
glossary.HRT: Makes the request, assumptions, scope, and ambiguity explicit.
glossary.HTML: HyperText Markup Language: the structural language used to describe web pages.
glossary.HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request-and-response protocol commonly used by web clients and servers.
glossary.ID: Identifier: a value used to name and distinguish one object from another.
glossary.IEPS: Produces tests, counterexamples, coverage, and evidence gates.
glossary.IETF: Internet Engineering Task Force: the open standards community that publishes RFC technical specifications and best-current-practice documents.
glossary.IURM: Chooses useful controlled variations that reduce uncertainty.
glossary.JPEG: Joint Photographic Experts Group image: a compressed bitmap format commonly used for photographs.
glossary.JSON: JavaScript Object Notation: a text format for structured data made from objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null values.
glossary.JSONL: JSON Lines: a log-friendly format with one complete JSON value on each line.
glossary.L0: Evidence or risk level 0: the lowest project level, normally suitable for observation or automatic handling.
glossary.L1: Evidence or risk level 1: a bounded level that requires stronger policy and evidence than simple observation.
glossary.L2: Evidence or risk level 2: a higher-impact level requiring grounded evidence, counterexamples, and explicit human review unless exact authority says otherwise.
glossary.L0-L2: The project evidence or risk ladder from low-impact observation through higher-impact work requiring stronger evidence and review.
glossary.LRU: Least Recently Used: a cache policy that removes the items that have gone unused for the longest time.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and structured external context.
glossary.MVD: Minimum Viable Design: the smallest design that still satisfies the declared constraints and learning objective.
glossary.NASA: National Aeronautics and Space Administration: the United States civil space agency, which publishes systems-engineering guidance used here as a lifecycle reference.
glossary.NIST: National Institute of Standards and Technology: a United States public agency that publishes technical guidance on measurement, security, risk, and trustworthy systems.
glossary.OBJ: Wavefront OBJ: a text-based file format for polygonal 3D geometry.
glossary.OFAT: One Factor At a Time: an experiment strategy that varies one input while holding the others steady.
glossary.OIEC-STM: Operationally Isolated Epistemic Control State-Transition Model: this project's bounded control layer for deciding whether a proposed state transition may proceed.
glossary.OURD: Decomposes a problem into orthogonal, uniquely identified relational components and the relations between them.
glossary.PEP: A design document used to specify Python changes and conventions.
glossary.PLY: Polygon File Format: a format for storing 3D meshes and point-cloud attributes.
glossary.PNG: Portable Network Graphics: a lossless bitmap image format with transparency support.
glossary.PTY: Pseudo-terminal: a software endpoint that behaves like a terminal so another program can control interactive command-line processes.
glossary.RFC: Request for Comments: a published technical specification or best-current-practice document in the Internet standards process.
glossary.README: The conventional project overview file that explains purpose, setup, usage, and important repository guidance; the name is a filename label rather than an acronym.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: libraries, tools, examples, and documentation used to build software against a platform.
glossary.SHA-256: Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit: a function that produces a fixed-size digest used here to identify and verify exact content.
glossary.SQL: Structured Query Language: a language for storing, querying, and updating relational data.
glossary.SQLite: A compact relational database engine stored in a local file rather than a separate database server.
glossary.SSDF: Secure Software Development Framework: NIST guidance for integrating secure practices into the software lifecycle.
glossary.STL: Stereolithography file format: a widely used representation of triangulated 3D surfaces.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: XML-based vector artwork that can remain sharp at any size and can be manipulated with JavaScript.
glossary.TCP: Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable ordered transport protocol used by many network applications.
glossary.UI: User Interface: the controls and information through which a person interacts with a system.
glossary.URL: Uniform Resource Locator: the address used to locate a resource such as a web page or file.
glossary.W3C: World Wide Web Consortium: the standards community that develops technical and accessibility guidance for the Web.
glossary.WAI-ARIA: Web Accessibility Initiative Accessible Rich Internet Applications: W3C guidance for making interactive web controls understandable to assistive technology and keyboard users.
glossary.XML: Extensible Markup Language: a text format that represents nested structured data with named tags and attributes.
glossary.X11: The X Window System protocol commonly used to display graphical Linux applications.
glossary.COUNT: A configuration field that limits or reports how many items are involved.
glossary.KEY: A configuration field or lookup name used to select a value.
glossary.MODEL: A configuration field that names the language or reasoning model to use.
glossary.SECONDS: A duration field measured in seconds.
glossary.TOKENS: A limit expressed in model tokens, which are small units of text processed by a language model.
glossary.OIEC: The governed architecture that separates understanding, evidence, authority, action, and learning.
glossary.STM: The bounded state-transition part of OIEC-STM-Agent.
glossary.SR: A bounded additive layer for generating and comparing reasoning candidates.
glossary.BD: Determines the supported boundary of a claim or model.
glossary.DL: Restricts active dimensions to a tractable and justified set.
glossary.SAA: Represents, qualifies, searches, and adapts reusable algorithmic structures.
glossary.PEP 517: The Python standard that defines a build-system interface for source trees and frontend tools.
glossary.EGL: A platform interface used to create graphics contexts, including headless contexts.
glossary.ABI: A binary-level compatibility contract between compiled components.
